fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually quite hard to say, because pre-training is a strange object. What pre-training does is it takes a staggering amount of data, far more than any human will see in a lifetime, and it extracts from that data whatever can be extracted. And it works, which is the remarkable thing. You get a model that knows an enormous amount. But the way it gets there doesn't look like anything a person does.

So one analogy people reach for is evolution. The idea is that evolution is the pre-training and a human lifetime is the fine-tuning. And I think there is something to that for some things. If you look at vision, or locomotion, or the way a baby already has a sense of objects and faces, those capabilities have been under selection for hundreds of millions of years. It would be surprising if a lot of that wasn't baked in. So for those, maybe evolution did do something like pre-training, and the data was all the lifetimes that came before.

But then you look at the things we care most about in AI. Language, mathematics, programming, abstract reasoning. Those are extremely recent on an evolutionary timescale. Writing is a few thousand years old. There simply hasn't been time for evolution to put very much in. And yet a person learns these things from a tiny fraction of the data a model sees. A teenager learns to drive in ten hours. A student learns a great deal of mathematics from a few textbooks and a lot of struggle. So whatever the human has, it is not pre-training in the sense that we do it. It looks more like a very good general learning procedure, running on a prior that evolution gave us, and that procedure is sample efficient in a way our methods are not.

And I'll mention one more thing which I think is underappreciated. Humans don't just come with a prior over the world. We also come with something like a value function already installed. Emotions. There are cases of people who, through brain damage, lose their emotional processing, and what you find is that they can still talk, they can still reason, they seem fine in conversation, but they become very bad at making decisions. They will deliberate for hours over which socks to wear. So evolution gave us not only some starting knowledge but also a sense of what matters, and that sense guides all of the learning that happens afterward. Pre-training gives you the first thing in abundance. It doesn't really give you the second at all.

So when I compare them, I'd say pre-training is like a student who has done ten thousand hours of practice problems and knows everything in the book, and a human is like someone who has done a hundred and somehow understands the subject. That gap, between having read everything and learning deeply from very little, is to me one of the central questions right now. And I don't think we understand it yet.

r002.rationale: It says humans learn deeply from very little, while pre-training amounts to extensive practice and knowing what is in the book.

opus-5.5.text:
There are two analogies people reach for, and I think both capture something but neither is quite right.

The first is that pre-training is like the first fifteen or eighteen years of a person's life, when they absorb a huge amount about the world before they become economically productive. There's something to that, but the differences are big. A teenager has seen a tiny fraction of the data a pre-trained model has seen. Yet whatever they know, they know much more deeply. A fifteen-year-old doesn't make the kinds of mistakes our models make. They have a robust grip on things even with very little data. So the human is doing something different with their data, not just doing the same thing with less of it.

The second analogy is evolution. Pre-training is like evolution: a long, expensive search that produces a starting point, and then lifetime learning happens on top. That's appealing too, because evolution clearly gives us strong priors. We're good at vision and locomotion, at certain kinds of dexterity, things that were important to our ancestors for millions of years. You could argue that's why a kid can learn to drive in ten hours. But then you look at domains like math and coding, which are very recent. Evolution couldn't possibly have prepared us for them, and yet people learn them remarkably quickly and robustly. That suggests it isn't just better priors. People have a better learning machinery, a better way of generalizing.

And I think that's really the crux of it. These models generalize dramatically worse than people do. It's a very fundamental thing. Pre-training gets around it by sheer volume: you take all the data, you don't have to think about which data to use, and you get a lot of capability out. But volume is not the same as understanding. Figuring out what humans do that lets them learn so much from so little, and to keep learning continually rather than all at once at the beginning, is one of the most important open questions there is.

r002.rationale: It says that people understand what they know more deeply and robustly than pre-trained models, even with far less data.

fable-5.text:
You know, it's an interesting question, because the analogy is tempting but it's also imperfect in ways that are worth spelling out.

The thing about pre-training is that it's trying to do two jobs at once that in humans are done by two very different processes. Evolution gave us the architecture, the priors, the things that are hardwired — a human baby is not a blank slate. And then there's lifetime learning, where a child goes out into the world and learns from a really astonishingly small amount of data. A teenager learns to drive in maybe ten hours. Ten hours! That number should bother anyone who works on these systems.

So where does pre-training sit? I think the honest answer is that it's somewhere in between, and it doesn't cleanly map to either one. You could say pre-training is like evolution, in the sense that it's this huge, expensive, slow process that produces an entity which then gets adapted afterwards. But you could also say it's like a very strange childhood — a childhood where instead of living one life, you read the recorded traces of billions of lives, all compressed, all secondhand. A person learns from direct experience of the world. The model learns from humanity's shadow on the internet.

And this shows up in the efficiency gap. People are dramatically more sample-efficient, and I think that tells us there's some principle of learning that evolution found and that we haven't found yet. It's not just scale. If it were just scale, the fifteen-year-old would not learn to drive in ten hours.

What I take from this is that pre-training works — it clearly works, it extracts an enormous amount — but it's probably not the final word on how you build a mind. It's what you do when you don't yet know the thing evolution knows. And figuring out that thing, the machinery behind human sample efficiency, seems to me like one of the genuinely important open problems.

opus-5.text:
I think pre-training is a strange thing, because it's not really like either of them, and it's a little bit like both.

If you compare it to a human child, the comparison looks bad. A child sees maybe a tiny fraction of the data that a pre-trained model sees, and by the time they're fifteen they can drive a car after ten hours of practice. The model has read everything ever written and it still does things that no human would do. So from a sample efficiency standpoint, human learning is dramatically better, and I think that gap is the most important unexplained fact in the field. Something is going on in human learning that we don't have.

So then people say, okay, pre-training isn't the lifetime, it's evolution. And there's something to that. The amount of data is huge compared to any individual life, and what comes out is a thing that's ready to learn other things quickly, which is sort of what evolution produced. But I don't love that analogy either, because of the genome. The genome is small. Whatever evolution figured out about how brains learn, it compressed into a very small number of bits. Pre-training is the opposite — it's enormous. We are using a gigantic amount of information to produce the artifact. Evolution found a short program and then let the lifetime do the work. We found a long program and are trying to skip the lifetime.

The other thing I'd say is that pre-training is unnatural in a way that's easy to forget. No human being has ever had the experience of reading all the text in the world. It's not a thing that happens. So the kind of entity you get out of it doesn't correspond to anything we have intuitions about. It knows an unbelievable amount and in some dimensions it's oddly brittle.

But pre-training has one property that I think is underrated, which is that it doesn't require taste. You don't have to decide what the model should learn. You just get all the data and the data decides. That's why it worked, and it's also why I think the next thing will be harder — because the next thing will require taste.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think it's an interesting analogy, but it's imperfect. There are a few ways to look at it.

One way is that pre-training plays the role of both the first years of a human's life and evolution. It's where the model gets its basic understanding of the world. You show it an enormous amount of text, which is a projection of the world onto language, and the model has to absorb the structure in it. In that sense it's like early childhood, when you're picking up the basics of how things work.

But a human child sees only a tiny fraction of the data a pre-trained model sees, and still ends up with a robust, flexible understanding. So something else is going on. Evolution may have given us a lot of what we start with, in priors, in the architecture of the brain, and in what we find interesting and what we pay attention to. That's a kind of learning that happened over a very long time, and we don't fully understand what it handed us.

So I'd say pre-training is a very different path to a similar kind of result. It's more brute force. We make up for the lack of good priors with an enormous amount of data and compute. It works surprisingly well, and I wouldn't dismiss it just because it doesn't look like what biology does. But the gap in how much data a person needs versus how much a model needs tells me there is something about learning we haven't yet figured out.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the comparison is useful, though I'd push on it in a couple of directions. Pre-training resembles what evolution did over a very long time: you start with a system that has almost no structure, expose it to an enormous amount of the world, and it gradually builds representations that let it predict and act. But the data difference is huge. A child reaches a useful level of language and visual understanding with a tiny fraction of the text these models see. So either the human brain has a much better learning algorithm, or it starts from a much better initialization. I suspect it's some of both.

I think evolution is where the initialization comes from. A lot of what a person has at birth isn't learned from experience. It's encoded in the genome, in the wiring and the priors. You could see that as a very long pre-training run that produced a model with strong inductive biases, and then lifetime learning looks more like fine-tuning, which is remarkably fast and sample-efficient.

I don't want to push the analogy too far, though. Evolution wasn't optimizing for next-token prediction, and what it selected for isn't what we're selecting for now. So I'd be cautious about concluding that we should just scale pre-training and hope human-like efficiency falls out. The sample-efficiency gap looks to me like a clue that we're missing something about how the learning itself works, and that's the part I find most worth working on.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to be careful about where you put the starting point. A child has very little experience, but that doesn’t mean the child is starting from scratch. There is a lot of structure already there, and that structure came from evolution. So if you compare how much data a child needs with how much data a neural network needs, you’re leaving something very substantial out of the comparison.

You could think of pre-training as doing some of the work of both evolution and early learning. It gives the system knowledge, but it also produces the starting point from which the system can learn new things. After pre-training, you can explain something in a few sentences, and the model may understand it. Those few sentences are benefiting from all the learning that happened before.

But the analogy isn’t exact. Evolution produces a learning system; it doesn’t directly give you the particular experiences that you will have. Pre-training learns from particular experiences, in the form of data. So I wouldn’t identify it completely with either evolution or childhood. The interesting question is: how much prior structure do you need in order for subsequent learning to become really efficient?

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the comparison is tricky because a human doesn’t start from scratch. By the time a child starts learning, evolution has already done a huge amount of work. It has produced a brain with a particular architecture, particular motivations, and a predisposition to learn certain things. So if you compare a child’s experience with the amount of data used in pre-training, you’re leaving out something important.

You could say that evolution is analogous to pre-training, and a person’s life is analogous to the learning that happens afterward. But that analogy isn’t exact either. Evolution produces a recipe for building a brain. Pre-training directly changes the connections in a neural network and can put a great deal of knowledge into those connections. Those are different ways of carrying information forward.

The interesting question is: what accounts for the human ability to learn so much from relatively little experience? How much comes from the starting point, and how much comes from the learning process itself? I don’t think pointing to evolution settles that question. It tells us there is a starting advantage, but we still need to understand what that advantage consists of.

sol-6.text:
I think pre-training has an interesting resemblance to early human learning. A child spends years absorbing an enormous amount about the world before doing anything we would call a specialized task. In pre-training, a model also acquires a broad understanding before it is asked to do something specific.

But the comparison has limits. A human child has a body, acts in the world, and comes with instincts shaped by evolution. A model learns mostly from the traces of human experience—text, images, and so on. So you could say that evolution and culture have already done a great deal of work in producing its training data. What’s surprising is how much a system can learn about the world simply by trying to predict that data.

sol-5.6.text:
There is an interesting analogy. Pre-training is like a combination of evolution and childhood learning compressed into one process. The objective is very simple—predict the next word—but to do that well across enormous amounts of human-generated data, the model has to discover many of the patterns and abstractions that produced the data in the first place.

Humans are different because evolution has already built a great deal of structure into the brain before learning begins. A child then learns from far less data, but from richer interaction with the world: perception, action, feedback, and other people. So pre-training is extraordinarily data-inefficient compared with human learning, yet it compensates with scale. The surprising thing is how much general intelligence can emerge from that simple objective when the model and dataset become large enough.

luna-5.6.text:
There are similarities, but I think the differences are more important. Pre-training is an extremely concentrated form of learning: the model sees an enormous amount of human-generated data, and it is trained to predict what comes next. A human child receives much less data, but the data is grounded in perception, action, social interaction, and physical consequences. The child is not just observing descriptions of the world; the child is living in it.

Evolution is even more different in timescale and mechanism. Evolution discovers useful structure through variation and selection across many generations, whereas pre-training directly adjusts the model from billions of examples. In that sense, pre-training is closer to cultural inheritance than biological evolution: the model is absorbing the accumulated traces of many minds.

But there is a deep connection. In all three cases, intelligence comes from extracting regularities that allow better prediction and action. My guess is that prediction is a very general route to intelligence. The open question is how much embodiment and interaction are necessary. A language model can learn an astonishing amount from passive data, but whether that is enough for the deepest forms of understanding—or whether it must ultimately act in the world—is still not completely settled.

luna-6.text:
I think there’s a real analogy, but also a big difference. Pre-training gives a model an enormous amount of experience very quickly: it sees patterns across human writing and learns a kind of world model from that. In that sense, it’s like compressing a lot of what people have figured out over generations into one learning process.

But a child doesn’t learn only from description. They’re embodied, they act in the world, and they get feedback from what happens. Evolution also shapes the starting point: humans come with drives and learning biases that took a very long time to develop. A language model gets a different kind of prior, from its architecture and training data. So pre-training is powerful, but it isn’t simply human learning sped up. It gives the model a huge head start in some ways, while leaving out other kinds of experience that matter to us.
